questions.q: On three voyages from 1576 to 1578, Martin Frobisher hauled tons of black ore from Baffin Island back to England. What did it turn out to be?
options: Worthless rock with no real gold in it
Rich silver ore that paid for later voyages
High-grade copper sold to Dutch merchants
Coal that fueled England's first ironworks
questions.explain: Investors hoped the ore held gold, but assays showed it was worthless; some of it was later used to mend roads and walls in Kent.

questions.q: In 1562 the Huguenot captain Jean Ribault planted a short-lived French outpost called Charlesfort at which present-day site?
options: The mouth of the Hudson River
questions.explain: Ribault left about 30 men at Charlesfort; they soon abandoned it, and the Spanish later built Santa Elena on the same island.

questions.q: After a storm wrecked his fleet on the Florida coast in 1565, what happened to Jean Ribault and most of his shipwrecked men?
options: They sailed home to France and were tried as pirates
Pedro Menendez de Aviles had them executed
They lived among the Timucua for the rest of their lives
They were ransomed to France for Spanish prisoners
questions.explain: Menendez killed Ribault and most of the Huguenots who surrendered; the inlet became known as Matanzas, Spanish for slaughters.

questions.q: Who commanded the French Huguenot colony founded on Florida's St. Johns River in 1564?
options: Jean-Francois de La Rocque de Roberval
questions.explain: Laudonniere had sailed with Ribault in 1562; he escaped when the Spanish took Fort Caroline in 1565 and later wrote an account of the colony.

questions.q: Which scientist on the 1585 Roanoke voyage wrote A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia, published in 1588?
questions.explain: Harriot studied the land, plants and Carolina Algonquian language; his report, later reissued with de Bry's engravings, promoted English colonization.

questions.q: In 1586, men under Roanoke's governor Ralph Lane killed which Secotan leader, who had also taken the name Pemisapan?
questions.explain: Lane suspected Wingina of plotting against the starving colony and had him killed, poisoning relations with the region's Algonquian peoples.

questions.q: How did most of Ralph Lane's Roanoke colonists get back to England in 1586?
options: Spanish ships carried them to Seville as prisoners
They built small boats and sailed north to join the Newfoundland fishing fleet
John White's supply ships arrived on time to collect them
They sailed home with Francis Drake's fleet after his Caribbean raids
questions.explain: Drake stopped at Roanoke in June 1586, and the hungry colonists left with him; a relief fleet arrived soon after and found the island empty.

questions.q: During his 1585-1586 raid on Spain's American empire, Francis Drake sacked Santo Domingo and Cartagena and then burned which Florida town?
questions.explain: Drake's fleet burned St. Augustine in 1586 before sailing north to Roanoke, part of the undeclared war that led to the Armada.

questions.q: In 1579 Francis Drake landed on the Pacific coast of North America and claimed the land for Queen Elizabeth I under what name?
questions.explain: Drake repaired the Golden Hind somewhere on the California coast and named the land Nova Albion, Latin for New Britain.

questions.q: How did Sir Humphrey Gilbert die in 1583, on the way back from his colonizing voyage?
options: He was killed in a skirmish with Spanish troops
He died of scurvy in a Newfoundland camp
He was executed for piracy in London
His small ship, the Squirrel, sank in a storm
questions.explain: Gilbert was last seen on the deck of the tiny Squirrel near the Azores; the ship went down with all hands that night.

questions.q: What became of Donnacona, the Iroquoian leader of Stadacona whom Jacques Cartier carried off to France in 1536?
options: He died in France before Cartier sailed again
He returned and led an attack on Cartier's fort
He became an interpreter for Samuel de Champlain
He was baptized and made governor of New France
questions.explain: Donnacona told the French tales of a rich Kingdom of Saguenay and died in France around 1539, before Cartier's third voyage of 1541.

questions.q: In the winter of 1535-1536, Cartier's crew at Stadacona recovered from scurvy after Iroquoians showed them a remedy made from what?
options: Fermented maize mixed with maple sugar
Dried bison meat ground with berries
The bark and leaves of an evergreen tree, boiled
Fish oil taken from St. Lawrence eels
questions.explain: The Iroquoians called the tree annedda, probably eastern white cedar; its vitamin C saved most of Cartier's men.

questions.q: Jacques Cartier sailed home from his 1541-1542 voyage with what he believed were gold and diamonds. What were they really?
questions.explain: The worthless haul gave the French a saying, false as Canadian diamonds, and dimmed royal interest in Canada for decades.

questions.q: Which Portuguese brothers sailed to Newfoundland and Labrador around 1500 to 1502, with both vanishing at sea on separate voyages?
options: Bartolomeu Dias and his brother Diogo Dias
questions.explain: Gaspar Corte-Real disappeared in 1501, and Miguel was lost in 1502 while searching for him; their voyages strengthened Portuguese claims to the cod coast.

questions.q: In a 1511 sermon on Hispaniola, which Dominican friar denounced the colonists' treatment of the Taino by asking, 'Are these not men?'
questions.explain: Montesinos's Advent sermon outraged the colonists, deeply influenced Bartolome de las Casas and helped prompt the Laws of Burgos in 1512.

questions.q: Which theologian at the University of Salamanca argued in 1539 lectures that Native Americans held real rights over their lands and rulers?
questions.explain: Vitoria's lectures On the Indians rejected claims that the pope or emperor owned the Americas and are often seen as a founding text of international law.

questions.q: What did the Casa de Contratacion, or House of Trade, founded in Seville in 1503, do?
options: Licensed and regulated Spanish trade and travel to the Americas
Trained Franciscan missionaries for New Spain
Judged appeals from courts in the colonies
Minted American silver into Spanish coins
questions.explain: The House of Trade registered ships, cargoes and passengers, collected the crown's share and kept Seville's monopoly on American commerce.

questions.q: Who became the first viceroy of New Spain, taking office in Mexico City in 1535?
questions.explain: Mendoza governed for 15 years, set up the colony's mint and royal administration, and sent Coronado north in 1540.

questions.q: Spain's New Laws of 1542 provoked an armed revolt by colonists in Peru. Who led it?
questions.explain: Gonzalo Pizarro's rebels killed the viceroy in 1546 before royal forces defeated and executed him in 1548; the crown then softened the laws.

questions.q: Which provision of Spain's New Laws of 1542 most angered the holders of encomiendas?
options: Encomenderos had to sell their lands and move back to Spain within a year
Native tribute had to be paid only in gold
Every encomendero had to pay the church a tenth of his land
Encomiendas would end at the holder's death instead of passing to heirs
questions.explain: By barring inheritance, the crown aimed to phase out the encomienda; after revolts it allowed grants to last another generation.

questions.q: In Spanish America, what was an audiencia?
options: A town council chosen from local settlers
A walled mission compound run by friars
A royal high court that also helped govern its region
questions.explain: Audiencias such as those of Santo Domingo, Mexico and Lima heard appeals and advised or checked viceroys and governors.

questions.q: An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed which Inca ruler around 1527, setting off a war over the succession before Pizarro arrived?
questions.explain: European disease spread ahead of the Spanish; Huayna Capac's death, and that of his heir, opened a civil war that left the empire divided.

questions.q: In 1572 Spanish forces captured and executed Tupac Amaru, last ruler of the Inca state that had held out in which remote mountain region?
questions.explain: Manco Inca had founded the neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba after his revolt failed in 1537; its fall ended Inca independence.

questions.q: In the 1570s, Viceroy Francisco de Toledo forced many Andean families in Peru to move into what?
options: Royal silver camps owned by the crown
questions.explain: The reducciones gathered scattered villages into Spanish-style towns, making it easier to collect tribute, draft mita labor and teach Catholicism.

questions.q: The patio process, developed by Bartolome de Medina at Pachuca, Mexico, in 1554, used what substance to pull silver from crushed ore?
questions.explain: Mixing ore with mercury and salt let miners process low-grade ore cheaply, fueling the silver boom but poisoning workers.

questions.q: In the Aztec Empire, who were the pochteca?
options: Priests who kept the solar calendar
Long-distance merchants who also gathered information
questions.explain: The pochteca traded far beyond the empire for feathers, jade and cacao and served the rulers as spies in foreign lands.

questions.q: Conquistadors were astonished by a vast daily market, said to draw tens of thousands of people, in which Aztec twin city?
questions.explain: Tlatelolco, on the island beside Tenochtitlan, held the largest market Bernal Diaz and his companions had ever seen.

questions.q: Archaeologists found skeletons of scarlet macaws at Chaco Canyon's great houses. What do the birds reveal?
options: Chacoans hunted macaws in nearby forests
Trade links that reached tropical Mesoamerica
Macaws once lived wild across the Southwest
questions.explain: Scarlet macaws are native to tropical Mexico and Central America, so their remains point to long trade routes into the Southwest.

questions.q: Which stone, mined in the Cerrillos Hills near present-day Santa Fe, turned up in tens of thousands of beads and ornaments at Chaco Canyon?
questions.explain: Turquoise was one of the most prized goods of the ancient Southwest, and Chaco's great houses held huge caches of it.

questions.q: Obsidian buried in Hopewell mounds in Ohio has been traced to a source in what far-off place?
questions.explain: Chemical tests link Hopewell obsidian to Obsidian Cliff in Wyoming, some 1,500 miles west, showing the reach of the Hopewell exchange network.

questions.q: In 1597 the Guale people rose up against Spanish Franciscan missions along the coast of which present-day state?
questions.explain: Guale warriors killed five friars; Spanish troops crushed the revolt, but the missions of the Georgia coast were rebuilt in the 1600s.

questions.q: In the winter of 1540-1541, Coronado's expedition fought the Tiguex War against which people?
options: Tiwa-speaking Pueblo towns on the Rio Grande
Comanche bands of the southern Plains
Apache groups of the Mogollon Rim
questions.explain: Spanish demands for food, clothing and shelter led to fighting in which Coronado's men besieged and destroyed Tiwa pueblos near present-day Albuquerque.

questions.q: What did Hernando de Soto's expedition suffer in its October 1540 battle at Mabila against warriors of the chief Tascalusa?
options: Heavy losses of men, horses and supplies, though it burned the town
A total defeat that ended the expedition at once
Mass desertion of its soldiers to the Native side
Capture of de Soto, who was later ransomed
questions.explain: The Spanish destroyed Mabila and killed thousands, but lost men, horses and most of their baggage, crippling the rest of the march.

questions.q: Hernando de Soto's expedition drove which animals along as a walking food supply, some of which escaped and spread across the Southeast?
questions.explain: De Soto reportedly began with 13 hogs that multiplied to several hundred; escaped animals are traditionally considered ancestors of the region’s feral hogs.

questions.q: The Florentine Codex, a twelve-book study of Aztec life written in Nahuatl and Spanish with Native scholars, was directed by which friar?
questions.explain: Sahagun and his Nahua collaborators spent decades recording Aztec religion, society and the conquest from the viewpoint of the conquered.

questions.q: Which veteran of Cortes's army wrote The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, decades after the fall of Tenochtitlan?
questions.explain: Diaz wrote his eyewitness account in old age in Guatemala, partly to answer histories that gave all the credit to Cortes.

questions.q: On the march to Tenochtitlan in 1519, Cortes and his Native allies massacred thousands of people in which city, a great religious center?
questions.explain: Claiming a plot against him, Cortes ordered the killing of unarmed nobles and townspeople in Cholula's main temple precinct.

questions.q: What did Pope Alexander VI's 1493 bull Inter caetera do?
options: Granted Spain the lands west of a line in the Atlantic
Declared that Native Americans could not be enslaved
Gave Portugal sole rights to all of the Americas
Called on England to colonize North America
questions.explain: The bull drew a line 100 leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde Islands; Portugal objected, and the Treaty of Tordesillas moved it west in 1494.

questions.q: The 1529 Treaty of Zaragoza settled a dispute between Spain and Portugal over which prized islands?
options: The Cape Verde Islands off West Africa
questions.explain: Spain gave up its claim to the clove-rich Moluccas for a payment of 350,000 ducats, extending the Tordesillas idea around the globe.

questions.q: Which West African empire, once among the largest in African history, fell after a Moroccan army armed with guns won at Tondibi in 1591?
questions.explain: Songhai controlled Gao and Timbuktu on the Niger; its collapse broke up the West African interior as the Atlantic trade grew on the coast.

questions.q: Brass plaques made for the Oba of Benin in the 1500s and 1600s often show which foreigners, who traded with the kingdom?
questions.explain: The Portuguese reached Benin in the 1480s; the bronze and brass plaques show them with beards, helmets and the brass manillas they traded.

questions.q: In 1576 Paulo Dias de Novais founded which city, the base of Portuguese Angola and a major port of the Atlantic slave trade?
questions.explain: From Luanda the Portuguese waged war on the kingdom of Ndongo; Angola supplied a large share of the Africans carried to Brazil.

questions.q: By the late 1500s, which captaincy in northeastern Brazil, centered on Olinda, had become the colony's richest sugar region?
questions.explain: Pernambuco's mills, worked by enslaved Africans, helped make Brazil the world's leading sugar producer; the Dutch seized it in 1630.

questions.q: Portugal's colony of Brazil took its name from what early export?
options: A tree whose wood yielded a red dye
questions.explain: Brazilwood was cut along the coast with Tupi labor and shipped to Europe, where its red dye was prized by cloth makers.

questions.q: In 1555, French colonists under Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon tried to found France Antarctique in which bay?
options: The Bay of Fundy, in present-day Nova Scotia
Guanabara Bay, at present-day Rio de Janeiro
questions.explain: The colony, which included Huguenots, was torn by religious quarrels; the Portuguese destroyed its fort in 1560 and drove the French out by 1567.

questions.q: Castile completed its conquest of the Canary Islands in 1496, a rehearsal for American colonization, by defeating which native people?
questions.explain: The Guanches of Tenerife resisted longest; the islands then became a base for sugar planting and a stop on Columbus's route west.

questions.q: Peanuts became a staple crop in West Africa after Portuguese traders carried them across the Atlantic. Where were they first domesticated?
questions.explain: Peanuts were domesticated in South America thousands of years ago and spread to Africa and Asia in the Columbian Exchange.

questions.q: Which flavoring, from an orchid grown by the Totonac people of eastern Mexico, entered world trade after the Spanish conquest?
questions.explain: The Aztecs received vanilla as tribute from the Totonac and used it to flavor cacao drinks; the Spanish carried it to Europe.

questions.q: Red pipestone, carved into sacred pipes and traded across much of the continent, was quarried for centuries at a site in which present-day state?
questions.explain: The quarries in southwestern Minnesota, now Pipestone National Monument, are still worked by Native people for pipes.

questions.q: Dentalium, a tusk-shaped shell traded far inland as a sign of wealth, came mainly from which coast?
options: The Pacific coast near Vancouver Island
questions.explain: Peoples of western Vancouver Island harvested dentalium from deep water; strings of it served as wealth from the Pacific Northwest to the Plains.

questions.q: In 1568, a Spanish fleet attacked John Hawkins's slaving ships at which Mexican harbor, hardening English hostility toward Spain?
options: San Juan de Ulua, near Veracruz
questions.explain: Only two of Hawkins's ships escaped, one of them commanded by young Francis Drake, who spent years afterward raiding Spanish shipping.

questions.q: Which 1604 treaty ended nearly two decades of war between England and Spain, three years before the founding of Jamestown?
questions.explain: Signed under James I, the peace freed English investors to back ventures such as the Virginia Company, chartered in 1606.

questions.q: In 1567, Juan Pardo's expedition from Santa Elena built Fort San Juan at the Native town of Joara, in present-day which state?
questions.explain: Archaeologists found the fort at the Berry site near Morganton; Native people destroyed it and Pardo's other outposts by 1568.

questions.q: Portugal's overseas expansion is often dated from its 1415 capture of which North African port?
questions.explain: Taking Ceuta, across from Gibraltar, gave Portugal a foothold in Africa and whetted Prince Henry's interest in voyages down the coast.

questions.q: The Foran Act of 1885, pushed by organized labor, made it illegal to do what?
options: Hire children under fourteen in factories or mines that shipped goods across state lines
Use convict labor on federal construction
Pay wages in company scrip instead of cash
Bring in foreign workers under contracts signed before they arrived
questions.explain: Also called the Alien Contract Labor Law, it answered unions' complaints that employers imported workers to undercut wages and break strikes.

questions.q: Besides Chinese exclusion, Congress passed a general immigration law in 1882. What did it do?
options: Required every immigrant to pass a literacy test in English
Set a 50-cent head tax and barred convicts and people likely to need public support
Set yearly quotas for each European nationality
Barred all immigrants who could not prove that a job and a place to live were waiting for them
questions.explain: The Immigration Act of 1882 was the first broad federal law screening arrivals; the literacy test came only in 1917 and quotas in the 1920s.

questions.q: In Republican feuds of the late 1870s and early 1880s, the Half-Breeds, who accepted moderate civil service reform, were led by whom?
questions.explain: Blaine's Half-Breeds clashed with the Stalwarts, who defended the spoils system and backed Ulysses S. Grant for a third term in 1880.

questions.q: In 1878, President Hayes removed Chester A. Arthur from which patronage-rich post, angering New York's Republican machine?
options: Collector of the Port of New York
questions.explain: The New York Custom House employed about a thousand people; Hayes's move was part of his push against the spoils system.

questions.q: Which editor of Harper's Weekly chaired the first federal Civil Service Commission, created under President Grant in 1871?
questions.explain: Congress soon cut off funds for Grant's commission, but Curtis kept leading the reform movement that won the Pendleton Act in 1883.

questions.q: Which German-born Interior Secretary under Hayes pushed merit hiring in his department and fought timber theft on public lands?
questions.explain: Schurz, a Civil War general and reformer, also sought to clean up the Indian Office and urged forest reserves decades before they were created.

questions.q: Why was the Tariff of 1883 nicknamed the Mongrel Tariff?
options: It was drafted jointly by British and American officials
It set different rates for each region of the country
It was passed by a Congress split among three parties
Its jumble of small cuts and increases satisfied neither side
questions.explain: A commission had urged real reductions, but lobbying left a patchwork that cut average rates only slightly.

questions.q: Which 1897 tariff, passed early in McKinley's presidency, raised average duties to the highest level up to that time?
questions.explain: Named for Maine congressman Nelson Dingley, it replaced the 1894 Wilson-Gorman law and stayed in force until 1909.

questions.q: In December 1887, Grover Cleveland devoted his entire annual message to Congress to which issue?
questions.explain: Cleveland argued high duties taxed consumers and piled up a Treasury surplus; the tariff became the central issue of the 1888 election.

questions.q: The Mulligan letters, used against James G. Blaine in 1876 and 1884, suggested what?
options: He had used his office to help a railroad in return for favors
He had sold navy contracts to a shipbuilder in exchange for stock
He had secretly promised to support free silver
He had taken bribes from the Whiskey Ring
questions.explain: The letters tied Blaine, as Speaker, to a deal with the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad; a famous one ended 'Burn this letter.'

questions.q: Republicans in 1884 chanted 'Ma, Ma, where's my Pa?' to attack Grover Cleveland over what?
options: Reports that he had fathered a child out of wedlock
His refusal to pay a Civil War pension
Rumors that he had abandoned a wife and children in Buffalo years before
His veto of a bill for widows of soldiers
questions.explain: Cleveland told supporters to 'tell the truth' and admitted supporting the child; Democrats answered, 'Gone to the White House, ha, ha, ha!'

questions.q: The Star Route scandal of the early 1880s involved fraud in what?
options: Contracts for carrying mail on rural western routes
Shipbuilding contracts for the new navy
questions.explain: Officials and contractors padded payments for mail routes marked with stars in Post Office records; President Arthur pressed the prosecutions.

questions.q: Why did the 1873 Salary Grab Act anger voters?
options: It cut Union soldiers' pensions in order to pay for higher federal salaries
Members of Congress raised their own pay and made the raise retroactive
It gave railroad executives seats in the cabinet
It ended pay for state legislators
questions.explain: The outcry was so great that the next Congress repealed the congressional raise in 1874, though the president's higher salary stayed.

questions.q: Which aged New York industrialist and philanthropist ran for president in 1876 as the nominee of the Greenback Party?
questions.explain: Cooper, then 85, won fewer than 1 percent of the votes; the party wanted paper money kept in circulation to help debtors.

questions.q: Before the Interstate Commerce Act banned them in 1887, railroad pools were agreements to do what?
options: Combine workers from several lines into one union
Build shared terminals in big cities
Share out traffic or profits to avoid rate wars
questions.explain: Pools let competing lines fix rates and divide business, but members often cheated, and the 1887 law made them illegal.

questions.q: An 1889 New Jersey law helped big business by allowing what?
options: Corporations to own stock in other corporations
Companies to pay workers in stock instead of wages
Railroads to set rates without state review
Banks to issue their own paper money
questions.explain: The law made New Jersey the home of holding companies; Standard Oil of New Jersey became one in 1899 as trusts came under legal attack.

questions.q: The Panic of 1893 began with the collapse of which major railroad in February of that year?
options: The New York Central and Hudson River
questions.explain: The Reading's failure set off a stock crash, bank runs and a depression that lasted for years; many other lines later went bankrupt.

questions.q: In the 1897 Maximum Freight Rate case, the Supreme Court weakened the Interstate Commerce Commission by ruling that it could not do what?
questions.explain: Without power to fix rates the ICC was largely toothless until the Hepburn Act of 1906 restored that authority.

questions.q: A violent 1892 strike by silver miners at Coeur d'Alene led to martial law and federal troops in which state?
questions.explain: Mine owners used guards and strikebreakers; after the clash, union men founded the Western Federation of Miners in 1893.

questions.q: In 1885 the Knights of Labor won a strike against railroads controlled by which financier, only to lose a bigger strike against him in 1886?
questions.explain: The 1885 win on the Wabash swelled the Knights' ranks, but the failed 1886 strike on Gould's southwestern lines began their decline.

questions.q: Which Knights of Labor organizer was named in 1886 to investigate the conditions of working women across the country?
questions.explain: Barry, a former hosiery-mill worker, toured factories and reported on low pay and long hours for women, one of the first such national studies.

questions.q: The Ocala Demands of 1890, a forerunner of the Populist platform, were adopted by which organization meeting in Florida?
options: The National Farmers' Alliance and Industrial Union
questions.explain: The Alliance called for a subtreasury, free silver, an income tax and direct election of senators, ideas carried into the 1892 Omaha Platform.

questions.q: Which Georgia Populist urged poor Black and white farmers to unite and became the party's vice presidential nominee in 1896?
questions.explain: The Populists paired Watson with Bryan, while the Democrats ran Bryan with banker Arthur Sewall; Watson later turned to bitter racism.

questions.q: Which Minnesota writer and reformer drafted the fiery preamble to the Populists' 1892 Omaha Platform?
questions.explain: Donnelly's preamble warned that the nation was 'brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin' by corruption and monopoly.

questions.q: What fateful choice did the People's Party make at its 1896 convention?
options: Nominating its own candidate, James B. Weaver, again
Merging with the Republican Party in the South
Endorsing Democrat William Jennings Bryan for president
Dropping free silver from its platform
questions.explain: Fusion with the Democrats gave Populists little in return; after Bryan lost, the party faded as an independent force.

questions.q: Nicodemus, Kansas, founded in 1877 on the High Plains, is notable as what?
options: A town settled by Black families from Kentucky at the end of Reconstruction
A Mennonite colony that introduced winter wheat
The first cattle town on the Chisholm Trail
A fort built to guard the Santa Fe Trail
questions.explain: Now a national historic site, Nicodemus is the only remaining western town founded by African Americans during Reconstruction.

questions.q: In 1866 Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving blazed a cattle trail from Texas to markets in which territories?
questions.explain: The trail swung west to avoid Comanche country, then north up the Pecos to Fort Sumner and on to Denver; Loving died after a Comanche attack in 1867.

questions.q: Much of the American cowboy's gear and vocabulary, such as lariat, chaps and rodeo, came from which earlier tradition?
questions.explain: Spanish and Mexican ranchers had worked cattle on horseback for centuries; Anglo cowboys in Texas borrowed their saddles, ropes and words.

questions.q: Kansas and other states restricted Texas cattle drives in the 1870s and 1880s because longhorns carried what?
options: A virus that killed wheat crops
A tick-borne cattle disease called Texas fever
Bison mange that spread to horses
Hoof rot that poisoned well water
questions.explain: Longhorns were largely immune, but ticks they carried killed local cattle; quarantine lines pushed the drives ever farther west.

questions.q: Which Colorado mining town boomed after rich silver-lead deposits were found in the late 1870s, making Horace Tabor a millionaire?
questions.explain: High in the Rockies, Leadville grew to tens of thousands of people within a few years; Tabor lost his fortune when silver prices crashed in 1893.

questions.q: Which Montana city, nicknamed the Richest Hill on Earth, became a leading copper producer in the 1880s as demand for electrical wire grew?
questions.explain: Marcus Daly's Anaconda company and others dug deep copper mines at Butte, feeding the wiring of the electrical age.

questions.q: The 1892 Johnson County War in Wyoming pitted large cattle companies against whom?
options: Small ranchers and homesteaders they accused of rustling
Chinese miners working on railroad land
questions.explain: Hired gunmen backed by big ranchers killed two men before being besieged; President Benjamin Harrison sent cavalry to rescue them.

questions.q: In 1878, which Virginia school, founded to educate freed people, began admitting Native American students in a federal program?
questions.explain: Richard Henry Pratt brought former prisoners of war to Hampton before opening Carlisle in 1879; Booker T. Washington taught Native students there.

questions.q: The Courts of Indian Offenses, created on reservations in 1883, punished what kinds of practices?
options: Selling liquor to soldiers at army posts
Traditional ceremonies such as the Sun Dance
Leaving the reservation to hunt bison
questions.explain: Interior Secretary Henry Teller's rules banned dances, the work of medicine men and plural marriage, part of the drive to force assimilation.

questions.q: As New York's street cleaning commissioner from 1895, which sanitary engineer dressed his sweepers in white uniforms?
questions.explain: Waring's 'White Wings' cleared streets choked with garbage and horse manure, a landmark in city sanitation.

questions.q: Which nurse founded the Henry Street Settlement in 1893 to bring health care to immigrants on New York's Lower East Side?
questions.explain: Wald's visiting nurses treated families in their tenements; she later helped found the NAACP and pushed for a federal Children's Bureau.

questions.q: In 1891 James Naismith invented basketball for students at what kind of institution?
options: A YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts
A Quaker women's college outside Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
An Indian boarding school in Pennsylvania
questions.explain: Naismith nailed peach baskets to a gym balcony to give young men an indoor winter sport; the game spread quickly through YMCAs.

questions.q: The Chautauqua movement, begun in 1874 at a lake in western New York, offered what?
options: Free hospital care for Civil War veterans
Night schools that taught immigrants English
Summer adult education with lectures, music and religious study
questions.explain: It began as a camp for Sunday school teachers; traveling Chautauqua tent shows later brought lecturers to small towns nationwide.

questions.q: In 1869 Lucy Stone and others formed the American Woman Suffrage Association. How did it differ from the rival group led by Stanton and Anthony?
options: It opposed votes for women in the western territories
It admitted only women who had been abolitionists
It refused to accept men as members
It backed the Fifteenth Amendment and worked state by state
questions.explain: The National Woman Suffrage Association opposed the Fifteenth Amendment for leaving out women; the two groups merged in 1890.

questions.q: In the 1880 election, Republican James A. Garfield narrowly defeated which Democrat, a Union general?
questions.explain: Garfield's popular-vote margin was under 10,000 votes, one of the closest ever, though he won the electoral vote comfortably.

questions.q: Horatio Alger's popular novels, such as Ragged Dick (1868), told what kind of story?
options: Immigrant families losing faith in America
Poor boys rising through hard work, honesty and luck
Union soldiers coming home from war
questions.explain: Alger's rags-to-respectability tales fed the Gilded Age belief that any determined young man could get ahead.

questions.q: George Eastman's first Kodak camera, sold in 1888 already loaded with film, was advertised with which slogan?
options: You press the button, we do the rest
Every family album deserves a better picture
questions.explain: Owners mailed the whole camera back to Rochester, where the company developed the prints and reloaded it, opening photography to amateurs.

questions.q: In 1890, with federal laws threatening the church's property, Latter-day Saint president Wilford Woodruff issued a manifesto ending what?
options: Church approval of new plural marriages
Church control of Utah's public schools
questions.explain: The Edmunds-Tucker Act of 1887 had seized church assets; the manifesto opened the way to Utah statehood in 1896.

questions.q: Virginia's Readjuster Party, which won power in 1879 with Black and white votes, wanted to do what?
options: Secede again if Congress raised the tariff
Cut the state's prewar debt and spend more on public schools
Return state railroads to private owners
questions.explain: Led by William Mahone, the Readjusters also abolished the poll tax and the whipping post before Democrats regained control in 1883.

questions.q: The Lodge Federal Elections Bill of 1890, which passed the House but died in the Senate, would have done what?
options: Required a literacy test, judged by federal officials, for all voters in federal elections
Allowed federal supervision of congressional elections to protect Black voters
Moved Election Day to the first Monday in October
Given women the right to vote in federal elections
questions.explain: Southern Democrats called it the Force Bill and filibustered it; Congress made no new attempt to protect Black voting rights for decades.

questions.q: A yellow fever epidemic in 1878 killed thousands and helped push which Tennessee city into giving up its charter for a time?
questions.explain: Bankrupt and half deserted, Memphis became a state taxing district in 1879 and then built a modern sewer system to fight disease.

questions.q: Which artist's paintings from the 1871 Hayden survey of the Yellowstone region helped persuade Congress to protect it?
questions.explain: Moran's watercolors and William Henry Jackson's photographs were shown to Congress; his Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone hung in the Capitol.

questions.q: Swarms of which insect devastated farms across the Great Plains in the mid-1870s, before the species mysteriously went extinct?
options: The Mormon cricket of the Great Basin
questions.explain: The 1874 swarms darkened the sky and ate crops, clothing and fence posts; the last live specimen was collected in 1902.

questions.q: What was notable about the Cherokee Outlet land run of September 1893?
options: It was the only land run open to women
It took place on land the Cherokee still lived on
It was cancelled after Sooners claimed every plot
It was the largest of the Oklahoma land runs
questions.explain: About 100,000 people raced for some 40,000 homesteads on more than 6 million acres the government had bought from the Cherokee Nation.

questions.q: Which 1928 disaster north of Los Angeles killed more than 400 people and ruined the career of engineer William Mulholland?
options: The collapse of the St. Francis Dam
The San Fernando Valley flood of the Los Angeles River
questions.explain: The concrete dam failed just before midnight on March 12, 1928, sending a wall of water down the Santa Clara River valley to the sea.

questions.q: Aldo Leopold's book A Sand County Almanac, published in 1949 after his death, called for what?
options: Building large dams to irrigate the arid West
A land ethic extending moral concern to soil, water, plants and animals
Opening national forests to more logging
Draining wetlands to create new farmland
questions.explain: Leopold, a forester who had pushed for the first wilderness area in New Mexico, became a founding voice of modern environmental thought.

questions.q: The deadliest tornado in U.S. history, in March 1925, tore across which three states?
questions.explain: The Tri-State Tornado stayed on the ground for more than 200 miles and killed roughly 700 people.

questions.q: After a 1928 hurricane drove Lake Okeechobee over its banks, killing more than 2,500 people, what did the federal government build?
options: A long levee around the lake, later named the Herbert Hoover Dike
A canal that would drain the entire lake westward into the Gulf of Mexico
A chain of storm shelters across the Everglades
questions.explain: Many of the dead were Black farmworkers; Zora Neale Hurston later depicted the storm in Their Eyes Were Watching God.

questions.q: The Labor Day hurricane of 1935, the most intense ever to strike the U.S. mainland, killed hundreds of World War I veterans working on what?
options: A dam on the Tennessee River
A levee along the lower Mississippi River
A highway project in the Florida Keys
questions.explain: The veterans were in federal relief camps building the Overseas Highway; a rescue train arrived too late, and Ernest Hemingway blamed Washington.

questions.q: Why did the Forest Service introduce Smokey Bear in 1944?
options: To promote hunting licenses in national forests
To sell war bonds to families who camped
To protect black bears from poachers
To persuade the public to prevent forest fires
questions.explain: Wartime officials feared fires would destroy timber needed for the war; Smokey's slogan became 'Only you can prevent forest fires.'

questions.q: Under the Swamp Land Acts of 1849 and 1850, Congress handed federal wetlands to states on what condition?
options: That they keep the land as wildlife refuges
That they use the land or its sales to fund drainage and levees
That they give it to freed slaves as homesteads
That they lease it to railroads for 99 years
questions.explain: Tens of millions of acres, much of it in Florida, Louisiana and the Midwest, passed to states, which often sold it cheaply to speculators.

questions.q: The Guano Islands Act of 1856 let American citizens claim unoccupied islands that held what?
options: Sea turtles for meat and shell
questions.explain: Farmers wanted guano to restore worn-out soil; the act led to U.S. claims on dozens of Pacific and Caribbean islands.

questions.q: Why was the 1965 court ruling over a proposed power plant at Storm King Mountain on the Hudson River important?
options: It let a citizens' group sue over scenic and environmental harm
It banned all nuclear plants in New York
It made the Hudson a national park
It required Congress to approve every new dam
questions.explain: In Scenic Hudson v. Federal Power Commission, a federal appeals court held that the agency had to weigh scenery and the environment, a landmark for environmental law.

questions.q: In Sierra Club v. Morton (1972), over a planned Disney ski resort at Mineral King, which justice argued that trees and rivers should have standing to sue?
questions.explain: The Court ruled the Sierra Club had not shown its members were harmed; Douglas's dissent became a classic of environmental law.

questions.q: Protests in 1982 against a toxic-waste landfill in mostly Black Warren County, North Carolina, are often seen as the start of what?
questions.explain: Hundreds were arrested trying to block trucks carrying PCB-laced soil; the protests drew attention to pollution in poor and minority communities.

questions.q: President Taft fired chief forester Gifford Pinchot in 1910 after Pinchot publicly attacked Interior Secretary Richard Ballinger over what?
options: His plan to sell Yellowstone to a railroad
His handling of coal claims on Alaska public lands
His refusal to fight a wildfire in Idaho
His support for damming the Grand Canyon
questions.explain: The Ballinger-Pinchot affair split Republicans and pushed Theodore Roosevelt toward his 1912 run against Taft.

questions.q: California's Salton Sea formed between 1905 and 1907 when what happened?
options: An earthquake opened a new channel from the Gulf of California into the basin
Engineers dammed the Owens River to store water
A cloudburst filled an ancient lake bed for good
The Colorado River broke through irrigation canals into a desert basin
questions.explain: For about two years the river poured into the Salton Sink until the Southern Pacific Railroad helped close the breach.

questions.q: During the Great Baltimore Fire of 1904, why could fire companies from other cities do little to help?
options: Railroads refused to carry their engines
Their steam pumpers froze in the winter cold
Their hose couplings did not fit Baltimore's hydrants
Baltimore's mayor would not ask for help
questions.explain: The fire destroyed some 1,500 buildings downtown and spurred a push for national standards for fire hydrants and hoses.

questions.q: The Good Friday earthquake of March 1964, the most powerful ever recorded in North America, struck which state?
questions.explain: The magnitude 9.2 quake and its tsunamis devastated Anchorage and coastal towns and killed people as far away as California.

questions.q: In August 1969, Hurricane Camille struck which coast with some of the strongest winds ever recorded at a U.S. landfall?
questions.explain: Camille's storm surge leveled coastal towns such as Pass Christian, and its remnants caused deadly floods in Virginia.

questions.q: Before becoming secretary of agriculture in 1933, Henry A. Wallace founded a company to sell what?
questions.explain: Wallace's Hi-Bred Corn Company, later Pioneer, helped spread hybrids that sharply raised Corn Belt yields in the 1930s and 1940s.

questions.q: Which American plant scientist won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for breeding high-yield wheat that helped launch the Green Revolution?
questions.explain: Borlaug's disease-resistant dwarf wheat, developed in Mexico, sharply raised harvests in Mexico, India and Pakistan.

questions.q: Unlike western national parks carved from federal land, how was Great Smoky Mountains National Park created?
options: By transferring an old army reservation and its forests to the National Park Service
By taking land from the Tennessee Valley Authority
By accepting a gift of land from a single timber company
By buying private land with state funds and donations, including Rockefeller money
questions.explain: Tennessee, North Carolina, schoolchildren and John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s family fund paid for thousands of tracts; the park was dedicated in 1940.

questions.q: What drove the 'great plow-up' of the southern Plains grasslands in the 1910s and 1920s, setting the stage for the Dust Bowl?
options: High wheat prices and new tractors
A wave of cotton planters from the Southeast
questions.explain: Wartime demand and gasoline tractors led farmers to tear up millions of acres of sod that had held the soil in place.

questions.q: The Enlarged Homestead Act of 1909 doubled the standard homestead to 320 acres for what kind of land?
options: Dry land that could not be irrigated
Mineral land in the Rocky Mountains
questions.explain: Congress recognized that 160 acres could not support a family on the semiarid Plains, prompting a dry-farming boom.

questions.q: Why did Chesapeake tobacco planters keep clearing new fields in the 1600s and 1700s?
options: Laws required them to rotate land with neighbors
Floods washed away the old fields each spring
Native nations demanded the old land back
Tobacco wore out the soil within a few years
questions.explain: Planters let exhausted fields go fallow and moved on, a hunger for land that pushed settlement west and caused conflict with Native peoples.

questions.q: William Bartram's Travels (1791), an influential work of natural history, described the plants, animals and peoples of which region?
options: The Great Lakes and Upper Mississippi
The Southeast, from the Carolinas to Florida
questions.explain: Bartram's lush descriptions of the Southeast and its Creek and Cherokee towns inspired poets such as Coleridge and Wordsworth.

questions.q: In the 1830s, Henry Shreve led the clearing of the Great Raft from the Red River. What was the Great Raft?
options: A sandbar that blocked the river's mouth
A floating trading post run by the Caddo
A logjam stretching well over a hundred miles
A pontoon bridge left by the army
questions.explain: Clearing the jam opened the Red River to steamboats; the town founded at Shreve's camp became Shreveport, Louisiana.

questions.q: Who proposed the Appalachian Trail in a 1921 article, imagining a footpath along the eastern mountains from Maine to Georgia?
questions.explain: MacKaye, a forester and regional planner, saw the trail as an escape from city life; volunteers completed it in 1937.

questions.q: The Highway Beautification Act of 1965, championed by Lady Bird Johnson, aimed to do what?
options: Limit billboards and junkyards along major highways
Plant cherry trees along every interstate
Require rest stops every fifty miles
questions.explain: The First Lady's beautification campaign also planted flowers across Washington, D.C., and drew attention to roadside clutter.

questions.q: In August 1805, Meriwether Lewis crossed the Continental Divide at which pass on today's Montana-Idaho border?
questions.explain: Beyond the pass Lewis saw range after range of mountains, not the easy portage to the Columbia that Jefferson had hoped for.

questions.q: After the 1913 flood devastated Dayton, Ohio, engineer Arthur Morgan designed a flood-control system built around what?
options: A ring of levees around the downtown
Dry dams that hold back water only during floods
A canal diverting the Miami River to Lake Erie
Reservoirs that stay full all year for power
questions.explain: The Miami Conservancy District's five dry dams have protected the valley since the 1920s; Morgan later became the first chairman of the TVA.

questions.q: After the home of attorney Z. Alexander Looby was bombed in April 1960, which Nashville mayor admitted that lunch counter segregation was wrong?
questions.explain: Pressed by Diane Nash on the courthouse steps, West agreed; within weeks Nashville's downtown lunch counters began serving Black customers.

questions.q: In Sweatt v. Painter (1950), the Supreme Court ordered which university's law school to admit Heman Sweatt?
questions.explain: The Court found a hastily created Black law school could not be equal, a step toward Brown v. Board of Education.

questions.q: Byron De La Beckwith, who murdered civil rights leader Medgar Evers in 1963, was finally convicted in what year?
questions.explain: Two all-white juries had deadlocked in 1964; new evidence led to a third trial in Mississippi and a life sentence.

questions.q: Educator Septima Clark is best known for developing what?
options: The legal strategy behind Brown v. Board of Education
The first Black studies program at a Southern university
Freedom songs that were sung at mass meetings across the Deep South
Citizenship Schools that taught adults to read and register to vote
questions.explain: Begun on the Sea Islands with the Highlander Folk School, the schools later spread across the South under the SCLC.

questions.q: What happened to James Meredith on the second day of his 1966 March Against Fear in Mississippi?
options: State troopers jailed him for parading
A sniper shot and wounded him
He was attacked by police dogs
He collapsed from heat and quit
questions.explain: King, Stokely Carmichael and others took up the march while Meredith recovered, and he rejoined it before it reached Jackson.

questions.q: In 1966, King moved his family into an apartment on Chicago's West Side to campaign against what?
options: Police violence at the Democratic convention
Low wages for city garbage collectors
questions.explain: Marchers in white neighborhoods met rocks and bottles; the campaign won a limited agreement and helped lead to the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

questions.q: The Lowndes County Freedom Organization, founded in Alabama in the mid-1960s, adopted what symbol, later borrowed by activists in Oakland?
questions.explain: Organized with SNCC's help, the independent party chose the panther because Alabama required party emblems for voters who could not read.

questions.q: In 1958, while signing copies of his first book in a Harlem department store, King was nearly killed when what happened?
options: A woman stabbed him in the chest with a letter opener
A gunman fired at him through the window
A bomb exploded near the entrance
A car struck him outside the store
questions.explain: Surgeons removed the blade, which had come close to his aorta; King said he felt no ill will toward his mentally ill attacker.

questions.q: What happened to King's home in Montgomery on January 30, 1956, during the bus boycott?
options: It was seized by the city for unpaid taxes
It burned after a kitchen fire
It was bombed while his wife and baby daughter were inside
It was raided by state police looking for boycott records
questions.explain: No one was hurt; King calmed an angry crowd outside, urging them to answer hatred with love.

questions.q: In October 1960, after King was jailed in Georgia, how did John F. Kennedy win notice among Black voters?
options: He flew to Atlanta to visit King in jail
He promised to name King to his cabinet
He telephoned Coretta Scott King to express concern
questions.explain: Robert Kennedy also called the judge, and King was released; the episode was publicized in Black churches before the close election.

questions.q: In 1963, which attorney general approved FBI wiretaps on Martin Luther King Jr.'s telephones?
questions.explain: J. Edgar Hoover claimed King's advisers had communist ties; the surveillance, later exposed by a Senate committee, went far beyond its stated purpose.

questions.q: Which SCLC aide co-led the March 7, 1965, Selma march that state troopers attacked at the Edmund Pettus Bridge?
questions.explain: Williams and SNCC's chairman walked at the head of the column on what became known as Bloody Sunday.

questions.q: Which SCLC organizer recruited Birmingham schoolchildren for the 1963 Children's Crusade?
questions.explain: Bevel argued that young people could fill the jails without costing families their jobs; images of police attacking them shocked the nation.

questions.q: Which NAACP lawyer, who won nine of the ten cases she argued before the Supreme Court, became the first Black woman federal judge in 1966?
questions.explain: Motley argued James Meredith's case against the University of Mississippi; President Johnson named her to the federal bench in New York.

questions.q: In Green v. County School Board of New Kent County (1968), the Supreme Court rejected what kind of desegregation plan?
options: Court-ordered busing of students across city and suburban district lines
Freedom of choice plans that left schools largely segregated
Closing public schools to avoid integration
questions.explain: The Court said districts had a duty to end dual systems now, judging plans by results rather than by promises.

questions.q: Which Washington police officer, assigned to guard Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, left his post during the play?
questions.explain: Parker reportedly went to a nearby tavern at intermission; charges against him for neglect of duty were later dropped.

questions.q: Which senator's daughter joined the Lincolns in the presidential box at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865?
questions.explain: Harris, daughter of New York senator Ira Harris, came with her fiance; the couple accepted after the Grants and others declined.

questions.q: In November 1863, Lincoln watched John Wilkes Booth perform at Ford's Theatre in which play?
questions.explain: Lincoln enjoyed the theater and saw many plays during the war; this was one of the few times he saw his future assassin on stage.

questions.q: By what route did John Wilkes Booth escape from Washington on the night of the assassination?
options: Across the Navy Yard Bridge over the Anacostia River into Maryland
Down the Potomac by rowboat to Alexandria
North on a train from the Baltimore and Ohio depot
Across the Long Bridge into Virginia
questions.explain: A sentry let Booth cross despite the wartime curfew; David Herold followed minutes later and joined him in southern Maryland.

questions.q: Which Confederate agent hid Booth and his companion in a Maryland pine thicket for days and then helped them cross the Potomac?
questions.explain: Jones brought food and newspapers while troops searched nearby and gave them a boat to cross the Potomac; he was held for weeks but never tried.

questions.q: The platform hastily built in 1865 to hold Lincoln's coffin at the Capitol has been used since for what purpose?
options: Supporting the caskets of those who lie in state
Carrying the Liberty Bell on tour
questions.explain: The Lincoln Catafalque, a simple pine frame draped in black, is kept beneath the Capitol and brought out for state funerals.

questions.q: When John Surratt was finally tried in 1867, before a civilian jury, what was the outcome?
options: He was convicted and hanged at the Arsenal
The jury could not agree, and he went free
He was sentenced to life at Fort Jefferson
He was acquitted by a unanimous vote
questions.explain: The jury split eight to four for acquittal; the government dropped the charges, and Surratt later lectured about the plot.

questions.q: Who was badly injured trying to stop Lewis Powell inside the Seward home on April 14, 1865?
options: Thomas Eckert, the War Department's telegraph chief
Edwin Stanton, the secretary of war
questions.explain: Powell fractured Frederick Seward's skull with his pistol before stabbing the secretary of state; both survived.

questions.q: Where was Vice President Andrew Johnson staying on April 14, 1865, when a conspirator was assigned to kill him?
questions.explain: George Atzerodt rented a room above Johnson's at the Kirkwood but got drunk instead; a gun found in his room helped convict him.

questions.q: Where was John Wilkes Booth's body finally buried in 1869, after President Johnson let his family claim it?
options: The family farm near Bel Air
questions.explain: Booth's body had been buried secretly at the Washington Arsenal; he lies in an unmarked grave in the family plot.

questions.q: Which photographer recorded the July 7, 1865, hanging of four Lincoln conspirators in a series of images?
questions.explain: Gardner also photographed the prisoners aboard monitors in the Navy Yard; his series follows the execution step by step.

questions.q: What did the District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act of 1862 do?
options: Freed enslaved people in all border states
Freed enslaved people in the capital and paid loyal owners
Let each ward of the city vote on keeping slavery
Ended the slave trade but not slavery in Washington
questions.explain: Signed by Lincoln, it freed more than 3,000 people nine months before the Emancipation Proclamation; Washington marks April 16 as Emancipation Day.

questions.q: Louisa May Alcott's Hospital Sketches (1863) drew on her weeks as a volunteer nurse where?
options: In a field hospital at Gettysburg
On a hospital ship off South Carolina
At a Georgetown hotel turned army hospital
In a Union prison camp in Maryland
questions.explain: Alcott nursed at the Union Hotel Hospital in the winter of 1862-1863 until she caught typhoid fever.

questions.q: In an 1863 letter to the actor James Hackett, Lincoln named which Shakespeare play as one that nothing equals?
questions.explain: Lincoln wrote that some of Shakespeare's plays he had never read, but 'I think nothing equals Macbeth. It is wonderful.'

questions.q: In 1864-1865, John Wilkes Booth's older brother set a New York record by playing which role for 100 straight nights?
questions.explain: The 'Hundred Nights Hamlet' at the Winter Garden ended in March 1865, weeks before the assassination drove the actor from the stage for a time.

questions.q: Which U.S. division commander was captured after the July 1950 battle for Taejon and held prisoner for three years?
questions.explain: Dean, of the 24th Infantry Division, was separated from his men during the retreat; he received the Medal of Honor while still a prisoner.

questions.q: In April 1951 at Kapyong, battalions from which two Commonwealth countries held off a Chinese advance and earned a U.S. Presidential Unit Citation?
questions.explain: The 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and 2nd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, helped stop the push toward Seoul.

questions.q: Ethiopia's Kagnew Battalions, which fought under the United Nations Command in Korea, were sent by which ruler?
questions.explain: Haile Selassie, who had appealed to the League of Nations against Italian invasion, backed U.N. collective security in Korea.

questions.q: In January 1951, as war spending drove up prices, the Truman administration's Economic Stabilization Agency did what?
options: Raised the income tax to 90 percent on all earners
questions.explain: The freeze was later replaced by more flexible controls under the Office of Price Stabilization and Wage Stabilization Board.

questions.q: What did the Universal Military Training and Service Act of 1951 do?
options: Lowered the draft age to 18 and a half and set service at 24 months
Ended the draft and created an all-volunteer army
Required every high school to offer military drill
Drafted women into the armed forces for the first time
questions.explain: Passed during the Korean War, the law kept the draft in place for the Cold War; universal training itself was never put into effect.

questions.q: During the Korean War, how could many college men qualify to defer the draft?
options: By paying a commutation fee of three hundred dollars, as in the Civil War
By working on a family farm for a year
By joining a church that opposed war
By class rank or a score on a national qualification test
questions.explain: The Selective Service College Qualification Test, first given in 1951, drew criticism for favoring young men who could afford college.

questions.q: What did the Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act of 1952 give Korean War veterans?
options: A cash bonus of one dollar for each day served, paid in government bonds
Education, home loan and job benefits like the World War II GI Bill
Free land in Alaska for homesteading
Lifetime federal pensions for all who served
questions.explain: The Korean GI Bill paid a monthly allowance toward schooling rather than tuition directly, after abuses under the 1944 law.

questions.q: After the armistice, how many captured American soldiers chose to stay with their communist captors rather than come home?
questions.explain: Their choice fed fears of communist brainwashing; most of the 21 eventually returned to the United States.

questions.q: Concern over how American prisoners behaved in Korean camps led President Eisenhower in 1955 to issue what?
options: An order ending the draft of married men
A ban on prisoner exchanges in future wars
A pardon for prisoners who had collaborated
A Code of Conduct for members of the armed forces
questions.explain: The code's six articles tell captured service members to resist, try to escape and give only name, rank, service number and date of birth.

questions.q: In April 1951, which House Republican leader read aloud MacArthur's letter backing the use of Chinese Nationalist troops, days before Truman fired him?
questions.explain: MacArthur's letter ended, 'There is no substitute for victory,' openly challenging the administration's limited-war policy.

questions.q: Which chairman of the Joint Chiefs warned in 1951 that a war with China would be the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time, with the wrong enemy?
questions.explain: Bradley testified at Senate hearings after MacArthur's firing, defending Truman's decision to keep the war limited to Korea.

questions.q: Fighting out of the Chosin Reservoir in December 1950, how did U.N. forces cross a blown bridge at Funchilin Pass?
options: Marines built rafts from oil drums and towed their vehicles across the gorge
Navy helicopters lifted every truck over the gap
They waited for the river to freeze solid
Air Force planes dropped bridge sections that engineers assembled
questions.explain: C-119 cargo planes parachuted steel treadway sections, letting the column bring its vehicles and wounded down to Hungnam.

questions.q: Which Army chaplain, who died in a prison camp in 1951 after caring for fellow captives, received the Medal of Honor in 2013?
questions.explain: Father Kapaun stole food for starving prisoners and tended the sick; his remains were identified in 2021 and returned to Kansas.

questions.q: Which New York Herald Tribune correspondent won a share of the 1951 Pulitzer Prize for international reporting from Korea, the first woman so honored?
questions.explain: Higgins landed with the Marines at Inchon after overturning an order that barred women reporters from Korea.

questions.q: The long-running TV comedy-drama M*A*S*H (1972-1983) followed doctors and nurses in what kind of Korean War unit?
questions.explain: Its 1983 finale drew one of the largest audiences in television history; real MASH units saved many lives close to the front.

questions.q: The 1954 Geneva Conference was meant in part to settle the Korean question. What was the result for Korea?
options: No agreement, leaving the armistice line in place
Elections that unified Korea under the U.N.
A peace treaty signed by both Koreas
Withdrawal of all foreign troops from the peninsula
questions.explain: Talks on Korea collapsed in June 1954; the conference is better remembered for the accords on Indochina.
